newsitem.title: USA: Rock caused July crash in Pensacola - investigators.
newsitem.headline: Rock caused July crash in Pensacola - investigators.

text.p: The crash of an F-16 fighter jet into a residential area on July 11, which killed a 4-year-old boy, resulted from engine failure brought on by a piece of rock that chipped one of the jet's fanblades, Air Force investigators said Friday.

"On the leading edge of the blade, a piece of rock or concrete caused a nick, which developed into a crack, broke off and was ingested deeper into the engine and caused the engine failure during the flight" Air Force Col. Mark Welsh, the investigating officer, said.

He said the damage began as a crack measuring seven-thousandths of an inch -- too small to detect visually -- which enlarged, eventually causing a blade to break and be ingested by the engine. He also said the plane's engine had failed three times after takeoff from Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina before the blade broke and caused the crash.

The plane was flying from South Carolina to avoid Hurricane Bertha, which hit the North Carolina coast a day later. It was investigated for any foreign object damage before takeoff, said Col. John Rosa, 20th Fighter Wing Commander at Shaw Air Force Base.

Air Force investigators said the crash, one of a series of U.S. military aircraft accidents this year, was not the result of error by pilot Frederik Hartwig, who then was a captain and has since been promoted to major and resumed flying at Shaw. Hartwig did not sustain any serious injuries after he ejected from the plane about 200 feet above the ground.
"He is an outstanding aviator and officer. He is doing well," Welsh told a news conference at which the Air Force released its crash investigation report.

The crash killed Sean Cannon, 4, put his mother Robbin in a hospital with severe burns, destroyed one house and damaged several others. The Air Force has paid out $126,000 in claims connected with the accident.
Robbin Cannon has since left the hospital but her family has not released information about her condition.

Investigators said the doomed F-16 experienced its first engine failure at about 21,000 feet above sea level, when Hartwig was still far from Eglin Air Force Base, near Pensacola on the western end of Florida's panhandle.

He heard or felt a pop or bang and the engine wound down, prompting him to begin procedures to restart it. He decided not to fly to an airfield northwest of Pensacola because its runway was not long enough for an emergency landing.

Instead he headed for Pensacola Regional Airport and considered -- but rejected -- heading for the waters of Escambia Bay. The engine restarted and the aircraft's speed increased until four miles before the Pensacola runway, when the engine failed and then restarted again.

When the engine failed for a third time, investigators said, Hartwig chose what he thought was the least populated place the plane could reach to land. He stayed with the plane until 200 feet and then ejected. The F-16 continued for several blocks before crashing into the Cannon home.

Welsh said an Air Force investigation had deemed untrue eyewitness reports that two F-16s were seen circling Pensacola Regional Airport on the afternoon of the crash, prior to the accident, and doing mid-air acrobatics.
